metadata.title: The PISA 2003 Assessment Framework – Mathematics, Reading, Science and Problem Solving Knowledge and Skills

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is an assessment framework for PISA 2003 rather than an empirical analysis paper. It describes the intended international survey design: paper-and-pencil testing of 15-year-olds with rotated test booklets and a background questionnaire for students and principals, plus optional international questionnaires. Because no microdata analysis is reported here, the manuscript does not specify whether complex survey weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are applied in estimation. For any downstream empirical use of PISA 2003 microdata, analysts should apply the official PISA sampling weights and, where available, replicate weights to account for the complex multistage sampling and clustering; plausible values (for cognitive achievement domains) should be combined using the standard PISA approach.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a framework/report describing how PISA 2003 constructs and reports achievement scales (and how tasks are designed and scored), not a study that estimates student-level cognitive outcomes from microdata. As such, there is no analysis pipeline in which plausible values (PV) would be generated, combined, or imputed, and the document does not report any missing-data handling strategy for an empirical dataset. The absence of PV/missing-data methods is therefore by design: the report focuses on assessment definitions, item/task structure, and reporting scales rather than on statistical estimation from a dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The document specifies that PISA 2003 targets 15-year-olds enrolled in both school-based and work-based educational programmes, with testing typically administered to about 4,500–10,000 students per country and 5,000–10,000 students per country in the second cycle. It also describes that test items are distributed across rotated test booklets so that each student answers a subset of the total item pool, while each item is administered to nationally representative samples. No country-specific inclusion/exclusion rules for an analytic dataset are provided because this is not an empirical microdata analysis.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD framework specifies the conceptual and operational basis of PISA 2003, with major emphasis on mathematical literacy (as the in-depth domain), alongside reading and scientific literacy and an integrated assessment of problem solving as a cross-curricular competency. It defines each literacy domain in terms of functional capacities for real-life situations, and it details how tasks are structured (paper-and-pencil, rotated booklets, multiple item formats including multiple-choice and constructed-response). The framework also explains how outcomes are reported using proficiency scales (with a mean and standard deviation convention) and how item response theory is used to locate both students and tasks on a common difficulty/proficiency continuum. It further describes the role of context questionnaires for linking achievement to student, family, and school characteristics, and it outlines scoring and reliability considerations for open constructed-response items. Because no empirical model is estimated, no ML performance metrics are applicable.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a technical assessment framework rather than an empirical research article. Consequently, there is no analytic sample with a reported N, no PV combination or missing-data strategy for an estimation model, and no ML algorithms or predictive targets. The framework’s value is in specifying what PISA 2003 measures (domain definitions, task design, scoring, and reporting scales) and how results should be interpreted for policy and research use.
